outputs.L1: The invention relates to a system for generating electric power, comprising: an alternator (1) configured to be coupled to a drive system (7) and to supply an AC voltage to an output bus (10); a reversible AC/DC converter (2), wherein the AC bus (6) is connected to the output bus (10) of the alternator (1); an electricity-storage element (3) connected to the DC bus (9) of the converter (2); and a controller (4) configured to respond to a transient load-shedding or charging-impact state by controlling the converter (2) to collect energy from the output bus (10) of the alternator (1) and store said energy in the storage element (3) in the event of load-shedding, and to collect energy from the storage element (3) and inject said energy into the output bus (10) in the event of charging impact, the converter (2) being controlled so as to inject currents into the AC bus (10) of the alternator (1) to compensate for harmonic currents.
outputs.L3:
The invention relates to a system for generating electric power. The system includes an alternator coupled to a drive system, such as an engine or other prime mover, and the alternator is configured to supply an alternating-current (AC) voltage to an output bus. Electrical loads may be connected to this AC output bus and receive power generated by the alternator.

The system further includes a reversible AC/DC converter connected between the alternator’s AC output bus and a direct-current (DC) bus. Because the converter is reversible, it is capable of transferring electrical energy in both directions: from the AC output bus to the DC bus, and from the DC bus back to the AC output bus.

An electricity-storage element is connected to the DC bus of the converter. This storage element may include, for example, a battery, a supercapacitor, or another suitable energy-storage device. The storage element can receive energy from the alternator through the converter, and it can also supply stored energy back through the converter when required.

A controller is provided to manage the operation of the converter and the storage element. In particular, the controller responds to transient events affecting the electrical system, such as sudden load shedding or rapid charging demands. During such events, the controller directs the flow of energy between the alternator output bus and the storage element. For example, when excess energy is present on the AC output bus, the controller may cause the converter to transfer energy to the storage element. Conversely, when additional power is needed on the AC output bus, the controller may cause the storage element to discharge through the converter to support the alternator output.

In addition to managing transient energy flows, the controller also operates the converter to improve the quality of the AC power delivered by the alternator. The converter is controlled to inject compensating currents into the alternator’s AC output bus. These injected currents are selected so as to counteract harmonic currents present on the AC bus, thereby reducing distortion and improving the waveform quality of the supplied AC voltage. As a result, the system provides both transient energy management and harmonic-current compensation, improving the stability and quality of the electric power generated by the alternator.
outputs.L4:
The invention relates to an electric power supply system, and more particularly to a system for stabilizing the output of an alternator-based electrical power source during transient operating conditions. In many electrical systems, an alternator supplies power to an output bus that feeds one or more electrical loads. When a large load is suddenly disconnected, commonly referred to as load shedding, the alternator output voltage may rise rapidly and produce an over-voltage condition. Conversely, when a large load is suddenly connected or when a battery or other storage device is abruptly charged, the alternator may experience a sudden current demand that can cause voltage sag, current distortion, or instability on the power bus. These transient disturbances can adversely affect sensitive electrical equipment and reduce overall power quality.

To address these problems, the invention provides an energy management arrangement coupled to the alternator output bus. The arrangement includes a reversible AC/DC converter, an energy-storage element, and a controller configured to monitor electrical conditions on the bus and regulate power flow between the bus and the energy-storage element. The reversible converter is capable of operating in a first direction to draw energy from the alternator output bus and store that energy in the storage element, and in a second direction to return stored energy from the storage element to the bus. The energy-storage element may include, for example, a capacitor bank, supercapacitor, battery, flywheel, or another device capable of rapidly absorbing and delivering electrical energy.

During a load-shedding event, the controller detects an increase in bus voltage or another indication of excess generated power. In response, the controller commands the reversible converter to absorb energy from the alternator output bus and transfer it to the energy-storage element. This action limits the rise in bus voltage and reduces the magnitude and duration of the transient disturbance. By providing a controlled path for excess energy, the system helps prevent over-voltage conditions and protects connected loads.

During a sudden load application or charging impact, the controller detects a decrease in bus voltage, an increase in current demand, or another indication that additional power is required. The controller then commands the reversible converter to deliver energy from the storage element back to the alternator output bus. This supplemental energy injection supports the bus voltage while the alternator responds to the new load condition, thereby reducing voltage sag and improving system stability.

In addition to managing real-power transients, the controller may operate the reversible converter to compensate for harmonic currents present on the alternator output bus. By sensing bus voltage and current waveforms, the controller can determine distortion components and command the converter to generate compensating currents. These compensating currents reduce harmonic content, improve waveform quality, and help maintain the power supplied to the loads within desired electrical limits.

The invention therefore provides an integrated transient-energy and power-quality control system for an alternator-based electric power supply. By selectively storing excess energy, injecting stored energy during sudden demand increases, and compensating harmonic currents, the system improves voltage regulation, reduces transient disturbances, enhances power stability, and increases the quality of electrical power delivered to connected loads.
outputs.L5:
**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the most common words in the English language, yet it is also one of the most important. It is called the definite article, and its main purpose is to point to something specific. When we say “a book,” we could mean any book. But when we say “the book,” we mean a particular book that the listener or reader can identify.

This small word helps make communication clear. For example, “the sun,” “the moon,” and “the world” refer to things that are unique or already known. In stories, “the” can guide attention: “The house stood at the end of the road” immediately suggests a specific house that matters.

Although “the” may seem simple, it plays a powerful role in English grammar. It gives sentences precision, connects ideas, and helps people understand exactly what is being discussed. Without “the,” English would feel less clear and much harder to follow.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent-style abstract for an invention involving an alternator, a reversible AC/DC converter, an energy storage element, and a controller that handles load shedding and sudden load increases while compensating harmonic currents.
counterfactuals.output: An electrical power system includes an alternator configured to supply an AC bus, a reversible AC/DC converter coupled to the AC bus, an energy storage element coupled to the reversible AC/DC converter, and a controller operatively connected to the alternator and the reversible AC/DC converter. The controller is configured to operate the reversible AC/DC converter in a rectifying mode to charge the energy storage element from the alternator and in an inverting mode to discharge the energy storage element to the AC bus. In response to a detected or anticipated load shedding event, the controller controls the converter to absorb excess electrical energy and thereby limit overvoltage or overspeed conditions. In response to a sudden load increase, the controller controls the converter to inject supplemental power from the energy storage element to support the AC bus and reduce transient voltage or frequency deviation. The controller is further configured to command the reversible AC/DC converter to generate compensating currents that reduce harmonic currents on the AC bus, thereby improving power quality while providing transient load management.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a technical description of a power generation system where an alternator supplies an AC bus, a bidirectional converter connects to a storage device, and the controller absorbs or injects energy during transient load events.
counterfactuals.output:
A power generation system may include a rotating alternator driven by a prime mover, an AC distribution bus, an electrical energy storage device, a bidirectional power converter, and a supervisory controller.

The alternator supplies electrical power to the AC bus at a regulated voltage and frequency. Loads connected to the AC bus may vary dynamically, causing transient changes in real and reactive power demand. These transient events can result in momentary bus voltage or frequency deviations if not compensated quickly by the prime mover and alternator control system.

A bidirectional converter is electrically coupled between the AC bus and the energy storage device. The storage device may include a battery, supercapacitor, flywheel, or other energy storage medium. The converter is configured to operate in both rectification and inversion modes, allowing power to flow from the AC bus into the storage device or from the storage device back to the AC bus.

The controller monitors system parameters such as bus voltage, bus frequency, alternator output current, converter current, storage state of charge, and load demand. During a sudden load decrease, excess alternator energy may appear on the AC bus, tending to raise bus voltage or frequency. In response, the controller commands the bidirectional converter to absorb energy from the AC bus and transfer it into the storage device. This action reduces the transient overvoltage or overspeed condition and stabilizes the bus.

During a sudden load increase, the AC bus may experience a momentary voltage sag or frequency dip before the prime mover and alternator can increase output. In response, the controller commands the bidirectional converter to inject stored energy from the storage device into the AC bus. This supplemental power supports the load demand, improves transient response, and maintains bus voltage and frequency within prescribed limits.

The converter may be controlled using current-regulated, voltage-regulated, or droop-based control modes. It may provide real power compensation, reactive power support, harmonic compensation, or a combination thereof. Coordination between the alternator voltage regulator, prime mover governor, and bidirectional converter controller allows the storage system to handle fast transient energy exchange while the alternator and prime mover respond to slower steady-state load changes.

In operation, the system improves power quality, reduces transient stress on the alternator and prime mover, and enhances the ability of the AC bus to support rapidly changing loads.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a patent abstract in formal language for a generator system that stabilizes an alternator output during load shedding and load impact using a reversible AC/DC converter and battery or supercapacitor storage, including harmonic current compensation.
counterfactuals.output: A generator system includes an engine-driven alternator, an electrical load bus, an energy storage device, and a reversible AC/DC power converter coupled between the energy storage device and the load bus. A controller monitors at least one electrical parameter of the alternator output and operates the reversible converter bidirectionally to stabilize the load bus during transient load conditions. During load shedding, the converter absorbs excess electrical energy from the alternator and transfers the energy to the energy storage device, thereby limiting overvoltage and overspeed-related output excursions. During load impact, the converter supplies supplemental electrical energy from the energy storage device to the load bus, thereby reducing voltage sag and assisting the alternator during sudden load application. The energy storage device may comprise a battery, a supercapacitor, or a combination thereof. The controller further controls the converter to inject compensating currents at selected harmonic frequencies to reduce harmonic distortion in the alternator output and improve power quality.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
